Succoth
SUK-koth
proper noun
Hebrew Sukkoth, “booths” or “shelters,” a town in the Jordan valley east of the river where Jacob built booths, and where Gideon rebuked the churlish.

See also: Succoth · Succoth

📖 Biblical Definition

Succoth, “booths,” took its name from the shelters Jacob raised there on his return from Padan-aram: “And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him an house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Succoth” (Gen 33:17). It lay in the valley of Jordan, a stage on the pilgrim’s road home. Long after, in the days of the judges, Succoth showed a harder face. When Gideon pursued the kings of Midian, faint yet pursuing, he asked bread of its men: “Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they be faint” (Jdg 8:5). But the princes of Succoth mocked him and refused, fearing to take his part before the victory was sure. Gideon returned triumphant and kept his word of chastisement: “he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth” (Jdg 8:16). The valley of Succoth was reckoned among the LORD’s own portions: “I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth” (Psa 60:6). Succoth preaches two lessons in one place: the shelter of the pilgrim who trusts God on the road home, and the folly of the coward who withholds his bread from the LORD’s cause until he sees which way the battle turns. Faith feeds the servant of God before the victory; unbelief calculates and is chastised.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town in the Jordan valley where Jacob built booths (Gen 33:17) and Gideon chastised the churlish (Jdg 8:5,16); a place of the pilgrim’s shelter and a warning against cowardly calculation in the LORD’s cause.

SUCCOTH, “booths,” a town in the Jordan valley east of the river.

Named for the shelters Jacob built on his return (Gen 33:17).

Its princes refused bread to faint Gideon (Jdg 8:5).

Gideon chastised its elders with thorns and briers (Jdg 8:16).

Reckoned among the LORD’s own portions (Psa 60:6).

📖 Key Scripture

Gen 33:17 — "And Jacob journeyed to Succoth, and built him an house, and made booths for his cattle: therefore the name of the place is called Succoth."

Jdg 8:5 — "And he said unto the men of Succoth, Give, I pray you, loaves of bread unto the people that follow me; for they be faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian."

Jdg 8:16 — "And he took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth."

Psa 60:6 — "God hath spoken in his holiness; I will rejoice, I will divide Shechem, and mete out the valley of Succoth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Jordan-valley town of Jacob’s booths and Gideon’s rebuke; the entry recovers the shelter of the trusting pilgrim and warns against cowardly calculation in God’s cause.

expand to see more

Succoth rebukes the cowardly prudence of the men who refused Gideon bread. They would not commit themselves to the LORD’s champion until the victory was certain, fearing Midian’s vengeance more than God’s displeasure. It is the eternal calculation of the fence-sitter, who waits to see which side prevails before he risks a loaf.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that faith feeds and supports the cause of God before the outcome is visible, while unbelief hedges and is chastised. The men of Succoth wanted the reward of the winning side without the risk of the fighting side, and Gideon taught them with thorns. The disciple is called to confess Christ and support His servants now, in the day of reproach, not to wait upon the applause of the victors. Yet the same Succoth is where Jacob built his booths and rested under God’s keeping — a reminder that the pilgrim who trusts finds shelter on the road home.
